opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing I value most is his taste, and how disciplined he is about it. Kaiming has a very clear sense of what problem is actually worth working on, and he's willing to wait for it. A lot of people, me included at times, get pulled toward whatever is hot right now and try to squeeze out a paper. He doesn't really operate that way. He asks whether this will still matter in five or ten years, and whether it's simple enough that other people will build on it.

Simplicity is a huge part of it. If you look at ResNet, or later things like Mask R-CNN or MAE, the core idea is almost embarrassingly simple once you see it. That's not an accident. He pushes very hard to strip away everything that isn't essential. When we worked together, he'd often ask, "Do we really need this component? What happens if we remove it?" If the result still holds without it, the extra part goes. A method should work because of one clear idea, not because of ten tricks stacked together.

The other thing is how rigorous he is with experiments. He's extremely hands-on. He looks at the numbers himself, he cares about baselines being strong and fair, and he wants to understand why something works, not just that it works. When we were writing, he'd go over a figure or a table again and again until it told the story cleanly. That standard is a bit intimidating at first, but it shapes you.

And as a mentor, he gives you a lot of freedom while still holding a high bar. He doesn't micromanage, but you know he'll ask the hard question. For me, that combination of patience, simplicity, and rigor is something I still try to carry into my own lab. I don't always succeed, but it's the model I keep in my head.

r002.rationale: It names MoCo and MAE only as examples of simple ideas; it does not distinguish collaborators’ improvements from Kaiming’s essential direction of those projects.

r003.rationale: It says Kaiming gives mentees freedom while holding a high bar, but does not identify making people around him more capable as what makes him an effective manager.

fable-5.1.text:
What I value most about Kaiming is that he's genuinely principled about simplicity, and he lives that principle rather than just talking about it. When we worked together at FAIR, I noticed he would almost never let a project ship with a complicated story. If something worked but we couldn't explain why in one or two clean sentences, he'd keep pushing until either the explanation became clear or the extra pieces were stripped away. ResNet is the obvious example, but it's true of everything he touches. The ideas look obvious in hindsight precisely because he did the hard work of removing everything that wasn't essential.

The second thing is patience. Kaiming is not someone who chases the leaderboard every week. He's comfortable spending a long time on a question that other people have decided is already answered, because he suspects the real understanding isn't there yet. MAE came out of that kind of patience. Everyone "knew" masked modeling worked for language, and there were many attempts in vision that sort of worked, but he kept asking what was actually different about images, and the answer turned out to be very simple once you framed it right.

And honestly, the thing I try hardest to carry over into my own group is how he treats junior people. He never pulled rank. When I was a fresh researcher he would sit with me and go through experiments line by line, and he took my disagreements seriously. He'd ask questions rather than give answers, and he'd let you be wrong and figure it out yourself. That kind of leadership makes people more confident and more careful at the same time, and it's rare. I've since had students of my own, and when I catch myself wanting to just hand them the answer, I think about how Kaiming would have handled it.

astra-6.text:
What I really value is his clarity of thought. He can take a complicated problem and identify the question that actually matters. And he’ll push you to ask: Why are we doing this? Is this component necessary? What does the experiment really tell us?

That sets a very high bar, but it also gives you room to think independently. The goal isn’t simply to make a system more complicated and get a better number. It’s to come away with a clearer understanding. That’s the kind of research leadership I really appreciate.

sol-6.1.text:
What I value most is his taste in research—the ability to identify a fundamental question and stay focused on it. In research, it’s very easy to add complexity, get a better number, and feel like you’ve made progress. He pushes you to ask: What did we actually learn? Which part is essential? Can we make it simpler?

And he gives you room to think. He doesn’t need to prescribe every experiment. A discussion might leave you with one very sharp question, and that question can change how you approach the whole project. That combination of independence and intellectual rigor is something I really value.
